text:
A vaccine lets the body practice fighting an infection without the deadly outcome of the disease.

Antigen fragments can come from inactivated virions, purified protein subunits, or mRNA that deltoid muscle cells translate into protein. The fragments drain to lymph nodes. There, dendritic cells escort them and display peptides on MHC molecules.

Helper T cells are selected from billions of randomly generated receptor variants, according to which one matches the epitope. They then give B cells the go-ahead to multiply inside germinal centers. Over two to four weeks, somatic hypermutation sharpens how tightly the antibodies bind.

Most effector cells then die. Long-lived plasma cells and memory lymphocytes persist for years, sometimes decades.

The payoff comes later. On genuine exposure, a secondary response starts within days, where the primary response lags by a week or more. It often neutralizes the pathogen before symptoms appear.

Aluminum-salt adjuvants, used since the 1930s, strengthen the alarm signal. Booster doses repeat the training, and immunity becomes stronger.
